title: Speak the truth, practice dharma
hookLine: an ancient teacher's graduation speech: speak the truth, practice dharma, and copy only our good deeds
tomorrow: "honor your mother as god, your father as god, your teacher, your guest"

cards: Caps, gowns, a stage, and someone at a podium telling a room full of graduates how to live. Graduation speeches are mostly forgotten by dinner. Here's one that's lasted well over two thousand years.
It's in a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya. A teacher has finished teaching the Veda to his student, years of it, line by line. The student is about to leave and start a life.
Before he goes, the teacher stands up and gives him his charge.

teach.b: First, the book. The Taittiriya belongs to the Black Yajurveda.

A later legend explains its odd name, tittiri, partridges: when Yajnavalkya, our friend from the Brihadaranyaka, quarreled with his teacher and gave back what he'd learned, his fellow students took the form of partridges and gathered it up.
Now the speech. It opens with three short commands that many Hindus know by heart: satyam vada, dharmam chara.
Speak the truth. Practice dharma: what's right, the duty that holds a life and a world together. And don't neglect your study.
Then the practical part. Bring your teacher the gift he'd value. Don't let your family line be cut off.
Don't drift from the truth, from dharma, from what keeps you well, from your own flourishing, from learning and teaching. And then a line you might not expect from a teacher.

teach.h: FOLLOW OUR GOOD DEEDS, NOT THE OTHERS.
teach.b: Whatever deeds of ours are blameless, those you should follow, not the others. Whatever good conduct is ours, honor that, not the rest. The teacher is admitting, at the graduation, that he isn't perfect.
And one more, for every hard moment after graduation.

teach.h: IN DOUBT? LOOK AT THE WISE AND GENTLE.
teach.b: If you're ever in doubt about what to do, he says, look at the people there who are wise, devoted, and gentle, and do as they would do.
Then the teacher seals it. This is the command. This is the teaching.
This is the secret of the Veda. After all those years, the secret is plain: tell the truth, do what's right, keep learning, and copy the best of the people who taught you.

how: The teacher's charge in Taittiriya 1.11 is recited in traditional Vedic schools at the end of study, and satyam vada, dharmam chara is widely quoted in Indian schools and at graduation ceremonies.

o: speak the truth: the teacher's first charge
a blessing the student gives his teacher
a vow of silence before leaving school

games.q: what's inside the charge — tap the pairs.
p: look at the wise and gentle

s: the teacher tells the student to copy everything he does
only his blameless deeds: those you should follow, not the others.
the charge comes at the end of the student's study
after the Veda is taught, as the student prepares to leave.
the Taittiriya's name is linked by legend to partridges
tittiri: a later legend tells of students who took partridge form.

games.q: you've graduated. one day you're unsure how to act, and your teacher isn't there. what does the charge say?
o: look at how the wise, devoted and gentle people there act, and do the same.
wait until your teacher can tell you.
games.why: look at those who are wise, devoted and gentle, and act as they would. the charge plans for the day the teacher isn't in the room.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something that mattered: a teacher, a parent, a coach, a grandparent. Let one of their good deeds come to mind, then, gently, one of their flaws, and hold both without judging.
Then let the flaw go, and keep the good deed.

wordCard.voice: Satyam vada, speak the truth. The first words of the teacher's charge, as the student leaves to start a life.

orig.note: Sanskrit satyam (truth) + vada (speak!): the charge's first two words.

carryVoice: Your line: speak the truth, practice dharma. Satyam vada, dharmam chara. Tomorrow, the next part of the same speech. Day three hundred eighty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Vishnu Purana 3.5 (the partridge legend of the Taittiriya branch)
